description: Hi everyone! My name is Farah Khalil, and I am a Primary Computer Studies Teacher at New English School in Kuwait. I am passionate about technology, creative problem-solving, and guiding students through hands-on STEM challenges—including coordinating student teams for global competitions like the NASA Space Apps Challenge. My core strengths lie in project organization, technical instruction, and turning complex ideas into clear, actionable plans.
summary:
Martian VR Command is a browser-based 3D Marswalk that turns NASA data into an interactive survival guide for future Mars explorers. Users pick a landing site from orbit (Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons or Valles Marineris), then explore on foot in first person. Assistant Farah, a voice guide, reads NASA findings aloud at each science stop.

Our layered Marswalk map combines several missions: routes and rock targets from Perseverance, RIMFAX subsurface radar, MEDA dust-devil alerts and a radiation heat map. The heat map is a schematic model scaled from Curiosity RAD measurements, and it shows explorers the safest shelter nearby. A survival guide compares radiation, air, cold, dust, terrain and water across all three sites. Checklists turn each walk into a science and safety mission. It runs on PC, tablet and phone.

This matters because the first crews on Mars must plan every walk around invisible dangers like radiation and dust. Our project helps them rehearse safely, helps planners see many data layers in one place, and gives students a field trip built on real NASA science, honestly labelled where models are used.
details:
What it does and how it works

Martian VR Command is a 3D Mars exploration app that runs in any web browser. Users start in orbit above a spinning Mars and choose a landing site: Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons or Valles Marineris. They then walk the surface in first person and aim at rocks and landmarks to open NASA science cards. Assistant Farah, our voice guide, reads each card aloud.

A live Marswalk map shows the user’s position, routes, science targets and the next stop. Its data layers can be switched on and off:

  • RIMFAX subsurface radar
  • MEDA dust-devil and wind alerts
  • A radiation heat map

The heat map models how much sky the nearby rocks block. It scales that with Curiosity RAD measurements: about 0.67 mSv per day on open ground, and about 4% less beside a butte. With one click, users can go to the safest shelter nearby.

A survival guide rates radiation, air, cold, dust, terrain and water at each site and compares all three sites. Checklists turn every walk into a science and survival mission, with an on-screen banner when it’s complete.

Benefits

  • Combines data from several NASA missions in one interactive view.
  • Makes invisible hazards like radiation visible.
  • Accessible: it works on PC, tablet and phone, has voice narration and needs no installation.

Intended impact

  • Future crews can rehearse a Marswalk and plan routes around hazards before stepping outside.
  • Mission planners can compare geology, subsurface, weather and radiation layers together.
  • Students get a free, classroom-ready field trip built on real Perseverance and Curiosity science.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
    • A-Frame 1.5 and three.js for 3D graphics
    • The browser’s built-in speech for Farah’s voice
    • Web Audio for wind and footstep sounds
    • Canvas 2D for the map, radar view and heat map
    • Pointer Lock for first-person mouse control
  • Development: CodeSandbox and standard laptops. No special hardware is needed.
    • Perseverance science results, including RIMFAX and MEDA
    • Curiosity RAD radiation measurements
    • Mars Odyssey THEMIS and MRO HiRISE images
    • NASA Mars Facts
  • AI assistance: we used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, test features and prepare our presentation.

Creativity

  • The terrain, rocks, dust devils and textures are all generated in code, so the app loads quickly with no large files.
  • We turned a static map into a walkable experience with a voice guide.
  • We combined real radiation measurements with a terrain model to show where an astronaut would be safest. This turns raw numbers into a decision a crew could actually make.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: every fact comes from NASA sources. Models, replays and schematic layouts are clearly labelled, so users know what is real data and what is illustration.
  • Accessibility: voice narration, simple controls and support for phones and tablets.
  • Performance: it runs smoothly in an ordinary browser.
  • The challenge goal itself: helping explorers plan a walk, stay safe and do new science along the way.
